[P1] 挪威民间故事
三只山羊
嘎啦嘎啦
整理／P.C.阿斯别约恩森 J.E.姆厄
图／玛夏·布朗 译／熊春 蒲蒲兰
二十一世纪出版社
21st Century Publishing House
11010065004037

[P2] 作者简介:
P.C.阿斯别约恩森（Peter Christen Asbjørnsen；1812-1885）和J.E.姆厄（Jørgen Moe；1813-1882）
19世纪中叶，受到格林童话的影响，开始搜集和整理挪威民间故事。虽不是作家，但他们称
自己是挪威民间故事的“编辑者和复述者”，将挪威口传之艺的本来面貌忠实地记录下来，是承过
《挪威民间故事集》等一批故事集。

玛夏·布朗（Marcia Brown）
1918年生于美国纽约州的一个牧师家庭，从小就随家人四处迁徙。她非常喜欢阅读、画画和
手工。据说每次搬家后总要先跑到社区图书馆办好借书证，并每天至少读三本书。大学毕业，当
了三年的语音老师。后来，为了专心学习绘画，只身来到纽约，一边在社区图书馆担任故事会讲
师，一边拜师学艺。在图书馆工作的五年间，她不仅在馆内接触孩子们，还经常走进社区给来自
世界各地的孩子们讲故事。这种经验为她后来的绘本创作打下良好基础。她意识到民间故事能帮
助儿童健康成长，因此她将世界各地的经典童话做成风格不同的绘本作品，本书也是其中之一。
她因其多才多艺而著名，每次画新书时都寻找最合适来表现故事的画面，因此她的每部作品的
风格和手法都不一样，她也因其不同作品先后获过七次凯迪克银奖和三次凯迪克金奖。

献给安·卡罗尔·穆尔和山怪

[P3] 很久很久以前，有三只山羊，名字都叫嘎啦嘎啦。
他们都想让自己长得胖一点，于是准备到山坡上去吃草。

[P4] 路上，他们必须经过一条河，河上只有一座桥，桥下却住着一个可怕的山怪，眼睛像盘子一样大，鼻子有拨火棍那么长。

[P5] 最小的山羊嘎啦嘎啦最先走上桥，
“吱呀！吱呀！吱呀！”

[P6] “谁呀？是谁把我的桥弄得吱呀吱呀响？”
山怪吼叫着。
“咩，是我，那只最小的山羊嘎啦嘎啦，我
正要到山坡上去吃胖一点。”小山羊小声地回答。
“是吗？但我正想把你一口吞掉！”山怪说。

[P7] “啊，求你别吃我，我太小了，过一会儿第二只山羊嘎啦嘎啦就来了，他的个头可比我大多啦。”小山羊回答。
“那好，你快滚吧！”山怪说。

[P8] 过了一会儿，第二只山羊嘎啦嘎啦走上了桥，
“嘎吱！嘎吱！嘎吱！”

[P9] “谁呀？是谁把我的桥弄得嘎吱嘎吱响？”
山怪吼叫着。
“咩，我是第二只山羊嘎啦嘎啦，我正要到
山坡上去吃胖一点。”第二只山羊大声地回答。
“是吗？但我正想把你一口吞掉！”山怪说。

[P10] “啊，你别吃我，等一会儿大山羊嘎啦嘎啦就来了，他的个头可比我大多了。”
“太好了，那你快滚吧！”山怪说。

[P11] 就在这个时候，大山羊嘎啦嘎啦过来了，
“吱—吱—嘎！吱—吱—嘎！吱—吱—嘎！”他
实在太重啦，桥发出巨大的响声，简直要断了。
“谁呀？是谁把我的桥弄得吱吱嘎嘎响？”
山怪吼叫着。

[P12] “是我！
大山羊嘎啦嘎啦！”
他的嗓音又粗又响。

[P13] “好，我正想把你一口吞掉！”山怪大声吼叫。
“好啊，来吧！我有两把弯刀，正好刺穿你的眼睛；
我还有两个巨大的石锤，正好把你砸成碎片。”

[P14] 大山羊说完，向山怪猛扑过去，
用犄角刺穿了山怪的眼睛，再用蹄子
把山怪踏成一片一片，最后又狠狠地
把他踢进河里。

[P15] 然后，大山羊也爬上了山坡。

[P16] 三只山羊越吃越胖，胖得都走不动了。
如果那些肥肉还没掉下来的话，它们现在肯定还是很胖的。
好了，“喀嚓、喀嚓、咚。故事讲完啦。”①
① 西方民间故事结尾的固定词之一，用来营造出从故事世界回到现实世界的氛围。

[P2] Author Introduction:

P.C. Asbjørnsen (Peter Christen Asbjørnsen; 1812-1885) and J.E. Moe (Jørgen Moe; 1813-1882)
In the mid-19th century, influenced by the Brothers Grimm fairy tales, they began collecting and compiling Norwegian folk tales. Although not writers themselves, they called themselves "editors and retellers" of Norwegian folk tales, faithfully recording the original oral traditions. They are known for works such as "Norwegian Folk Tales".

Marcia Brown
Born in 1918 in a minister's family in New York State, USA, she moved frequently with her family from a young age. She loved reading, drawing, and crafts. It is said that after each move, she would first go to the local community library to get a library card and read at least three books every day. After graduating from university, she taught speech for three years. Later, to focus on studying painting, she moved to New York alone, working as a storytime lecturer at a community library while also studying under masters. During her five years at the library, she not only interacted with children within the library but also frequently visited communities to tell stories to children from all over the world. This experience laid a solid foundation for her later picture book creation. She realized that folk tales could help children grow up healthily, so she created picture books in different styles based on classic fairy tales from around the world; this book is one of them. She is famous for her versatility, always seeking the most suitable visual style for each new book, resulting in each of her works having a unique style and technique. She won seven Caldecott Honor Awards and three Caldecott Medals for her different works.

Dedicated to Ann, Carol, Moore, and the Troll

[P3] Long, long ago, there were three goats, all named Gaa-la-gaa-la.
They all wanted to get a bit fatter, so they prepared to go up the hillside to eat grass.

[P4] On the way, they must cross a river. There is only one bridge over the river, and under it lives a terrible mountain monster, with eyes as big as plates and a nose as long as a fire poker.

[P5] The smallest goat, Galla Galla, went up the bridge first,
"Creak! Creak! Creak!"

[P6] "Who is it? Who is making my bridge creak and groan?" the troll roared.
"Baa, it's me, the smallest goat, Galla Galla. I'm just going up the hill to get a bit fatter," the little goat answered quietly.
"Is that so? But I'm just about to swallow you whole!" the troll said.

[P7] "Ah, please don't eat me, I'm too small. In a moment, the second goat, Galla Galla, will come, and he's much bigger than me," the little goat replied.
"Alright, then get out of here quickly!" the troll said.

[P8] After a while, the second goat, Galla Galla, walked onto the bridge,
"Creak! Creak! Creak!"

[P9] "Who is it? Who is making my bridge creak and groan?" the troll roared.
"Baa, I am the second goat, Galla Galla, and I'm just going to the hillside to get a bit fatter," the second goat answered loudly.
"Is that so? But I was just about to swallow you whole!" the troll said.

[P10] "Ah, don't eat me, wait a moment, the big goat Galla Galla is coming, he's much bigger than me."
"Great, then get out of here quickly!" said the troll.

[P11] At this moment, the big goat Galla Galla came over.
"Creak-creak-ga! Creak-creak-ga! Creak-creak-ga!" He was so heavy that the bridge made a huge noise, almost breaking.
"Who is it? Who is making my bridge creak and groan?" the troll roared.

[P12] "It's me!
Big goat Galla Galla!"
His voice was loud and deep.

[P13] "Good, I was just about to swallow you whole!" the monster roared.
"All right, come on! I have two curved knives, just right to pierce your eyes;
I also have two huge stone hammers, just right to smash you into pieces."

[P14] The big goat, after speaking, lunged fiercely at the mountain monster,
using its horns to pierce the monster's eyes, then stomped it
into pieces with its hooves, and finally kicked it狠狠地
into the river.

[P15] Then, the big goat climbed up the hill too.

[P16] The three goats got fatter and fatter, so fat they couldn't move.
If that fatty meat hasn't fallen off yet, they're probably still very fat.
Well, "Crack, crack, thud. The story is finished."①
① One of the fixed phrases at the end of Western folk tales, used to create an atmosphere of returning from the story world to the real world.
full_summary_zh:
[P1] 本页为绘本《三只山羊嘎啦嘎啦》的封面，展示了三只正在吃草的山羊，上方标有书名、整理者、绘者、译者及出版社信息。
[P2] 本页为绘本《三只山羊嘎啦嘎啦》的版权页，包含作者和插画师简介、献词、出版信息及版权说明。右侧配有一幅山羊的插图。
[P3] 本页讲述了很久以前有三只名叫嘎啦嘎啦的山羊，为了长胖而准备去山坡上吃草，画面展示了三只山羊在阳光明媚的森林边准备出发的场景。
[P4] 三只山羊在前往山坡吃草的路上，发现必须经过一座桥，桥下住着一个眼睛像盘子、鼻子像拨火棍的可怕山怪。
[P5] 最小的山羊嘎啦嘎啦第一个走上桥，桥发出吱呀吱呀的声音。
[P6] 最小的山羊嘎啦嘎啦走上桥，桥发出声响，桥下的山怪被惊动，威胁要把它一口吞掉。
[P7] 最小的山羊嘎啦嘎啦请求山怪不要吃它，声称第二只山羊更大，山怪同意让它离开。
[P8] 第二只山羊嘎啦嘎啦走上桥，桥发出嘎吱嘎吱的声音。
[P9] 第二只山羊嘎啦嘎啦走上桥，桥发出声响，桥下的山怪被惊动，威胁要把它一口吞掉。
[P10] 最小的山羊嘎啦嘎啦请求山怪不要吃它，声称更大的山羊即将到来，山怪同意放它离开。
[P11] 最大的山羊嘎啦嘎啦走上桥，桥发出巨大声响，桥下的山怪被惊动，愤怒地吼叫着质问是谁在弄响他的桥。
[P12] 最大的山羊嘎啦嘎啦走上桥，大声宣告自己的身份，声音又粗又响，画面特写其威严的头部。
[P13] 最大的山羊嘎啦嘎啦走上桥，与桥下的山怪对峙，山怪威胁要吃掉它，而山羊则毫不畏惧地宣告自己拥有武器，准备迎战。
[P14] 最大的山羊与山怪展开决斗，用犄角刺穿山怪眼睛，用蹄子将其踏碎，并狠狠踢进河里。
[P15] 大山羊成功爬上山坡，与另外两只山羊汇合，背景是阳光照耀的森林和山坡。
[P16] 三只山羊在故事结尾时因吃太多而变得非常胖，无法行走。画面描绘了它们在草地上吃草的场景，并以“喀嚓、喀嚓、咚。故事讲完啦。”作为结尾，附有对这一民间故事结尾语的注释。
